title: When Is a Steerable Concept Representation Real?Measurement Confounds in a Cross-Family Audit of Neuroscience Parallels in LLMs

paper.title: When Is a Steerable Concept Representation Real? Measurement Confounds in a Cross-Family Audit of Neuroscience Parallels in LLMs
paper.abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly reported to exhibit human-like neural and cognitive signatures, including concept cells, mental number lines, and cognitive maps. These claims often rely on linear probing and activation steering applied to a single model, yet both methods are highly sensitive to measurement choices. A reported parallel may therefore reflect the model, the measurement procedure, or both. We audit four representative neuroscience-inspired paradigms across 17 models from five families, spanning 0.6 0.6 B to 72 72 B parameters. Our main experiment examines the causal steerability of concept directions. With raw activation units and a fixed layer and coefficient, steerability appears to increase with model scale, resembling an emergent capability. However, this pattern is produced by an uncalibrated pipeline rather than by a claim established in the steering literature. The trend depends jointly on raw units, the readout metric, and the operating point; correcting any one of these removes it. With residual-norm-comparable interventions and held-out operating-point selection, concept steering remains significant at every scale, but shows no significant trend across the Qwen3 series, although the confidence interval does not rule out a moderate positive slope. The remaining results are mixed. A linear geographic world map is consistently decodable in every tested checkpoint up to 72 72 B. Number magnitude is strongly encoded, but whether individual neurons appear bell-shaped or monotonic depends on the selection criterion. Language-specific structure is localizable, but the direction of the cross-lingual asymmetry reverses under a different attribution method. These results suggest that the main constraint on AI neuroscience is not a lack of phenomena, but a lack of comparable measurements and adequate controls. We release the protocol, stimuli, and code.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: Same data, different ruler, different conclusion. Left: a standard pipeline makes concept steerability appear to increase with model size in raw activation units. Once the intervention is normalized across models and the operating point is selected on held-out concepts, no significant scaling trend remains. Right: the four neuroscience-inspired phenomena examined in this study and the conclusions supported after control analyses. A growing body of “AI neuroscience” treats large language models (LLMs) as systems whose internal representations can be recorded and perturbed. This literature has reported several parallels with biological cognition, including neurons selective for individual concepts ( Quiroga et al., 2005 ; Templeton et al., 2024 ) , linear representations of space and time ( Gurnee and Tegmark, 2024 ) , log-compressed number representations with Weber–Fechner behaviour ( AlquBoj et al., 2025 ; Nieder, 2016 ) , and emotion or concept directions that causally influence model outputs ( Sofroniew et al., 2026 ; Rimsky et al., 2024 ) . Together, these findings suggest that LLMs may exhibit representational structures resembling those observed in biological systems. Many such results rely on two methods: linear probing , which tests whether a variable can be decoded from activations, and activation steering , which tests whether adding a direction changes model behaviour. Both are sensitive to analytical choices, including how units are selected, how intervention strength is defined, which layer is used, and whether specificity and null controls are included. Moreover, most studies examine a single model or a narrow range of model sizes. This makes it difficult to distinguish model-specific findings from broader regularities, or genuine effects from measurement artifacts. Similar concerns have already been raised for emergent capabilities, some of which disappear under alternative metrics ( Schaeffer et al., 2023 ) . Here, we examine the same problem in a causal representational setting. We examine concept steering in depth and audit three additional neuroscience-inspired phenomena across 17 models from five families, spanning 0.6 0.6 B to 72 72 B parameters. Rather than asking whether these phenomena are “real” in an absolute sense, we test whether the associated claims remain stable under stronger controls and alternative measurement choices. For concept steering (§ 4.1 ), the apparent increase with model scale is not measurement-invariant: it depends jointly on raw intervention units, the readout metric, and a fixed operating point, and disappears when any one of these is corrected. With residual-norm-comparable interventions and held-out operating-point selection, steering remains significant at every tested scale, but shows no significant trend across the Qwen3 series. We formalize these controls in an audit protocol (§ 3 ) combining held-out selection, residual-norm normalization, specificity and null controls, and cross-family replication. Applied across all four analyses, the protocol yields a cross-model taxonomy (§ 4 ): linear geographic structure is consistently decodable up to 72 72 B; number magnitude is robustly encoded, but bell-shaped versus monotonic tuning depends on neuron selection; and language-specific structure is localizable, although the direction of the cross-lingual asymmetry changes with the attribution method. We further derive an efficient-coding account of monotonic magnitude representations under an idealized scalar model (App. A ) and release the protocol, stimuli, and code. 1 1 1 Anonymized: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ai-neurosci-audition-45CF (de-anonymized upon acceptance).

sections.heading: Cognitive parallels in LLMs.
sections.text: LLMs linearly encode space and time ( Gurnee and Tegmark, 2024 ) , task-specific world models ( Li et al., 2023a ) , truth ( Marks and Tegmark, 2023 ) , and number magnitude, reproducing distance/size/ratio effects and a log-compressed number line ( AlquBoj et al., 2025 ; Dehaene, 2003 ; Nieder, 2016 ) ; emotion, concept, and persona directions have been characterized and steered ( Sofroniew et al., 2026 ; Templeton et al., 2024 ) . These works establish that the relevant geometry exists. We ask which causal claims survive controls across families and scales.

sections.heading: Probing and steering.
sections.text: Linear probes read variables off activations ( Alain and Bengio, 2017 ) , but a decodable variable need not be one the model uses, which is why control-task baselines are needed ( Hewitt and Liang, 2019 ) . Steering methods add a direction to change behaviour: difference-in-means and contrastive activation addition ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ) , activation addition ( turner2023activation ) , inference-time intervention ( Li et al., 2023b ) , and representation engineering ( Zou et al., 2023 ) ; the linear representation hypothesis ( Park et al., 2024 ) underpins most causal claims, and factual edits localize to MLP weights ( Meng et al., 2022 ) . Crucially, the steering literature does not claim that steerability emerges with scale: Rimsky et al. (2024) report mixed effects at 13 13 B, and the one systematic cross-scale study ( Ali et al., 2025 ) finds that CAA effectiveness diminishes with model size. The apparent emergence our case study examines is therefore a natural default, not an established claim; because an unnormalized recipe can manufacture either an apparent rise or an apparent decline, raw units are not a comparable measure of steerability across scale. Superposition ( Elhage et al., 2022 ) , dictionary learning ( Bricken et al., 2023 ) , and cross-model convergence ( Huh et al., 2024 ) warn that decodable directions need not be the units of computation, a warning we operationalize. The reliability of steering vectors is itself an active concern, and our units argument gives one concrete failure mode.

sections.heading: Neuroscience anchors.
sections.text: Concept cells ( Quiroga et al., 2005 ) ; place and grid cells ( O’Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971 ; Hafting et al., 2005 ; Constantinescu et al., 2016 ) ; the geometry of abstraction ( Bernardi et al., 2020 ) ; efficient coding ( Laughlin and others, 1981 ) ; and bell-shaped number neurons provide the biological referents against which we score the models.

sections.heading: 3.1 Models and grid
sections.text: We evaluate 17 17 open-weight checkpoints spanning five developers, from 0.6 0.6 to 72 72 B parameters: Qwen3 at { 0.6 , 1.7 , 4 , 8 , 14 , 32 } \{0.6,1.7,4,8,14,32\} B and Qwen2.5- 72 72 B; Llama-3.2 at { 1 , 3 } \{1,3\} B, Llama-3.1- 8 8 B, and Llama-3.1- 70 70 B; Phi-3.5-mini ( 3.8 3.8 B) and Phi-4 ( 14 14 B); Ministral- 8 8 B and Mistral-Small- 24 24 B; and Gemma-2 at { 9 , 27 } \{9,27\} B. Qwen3/Qwen2.5 and Phi-4 are base (pre-trained) checkpoints; Llama, Phi-3.5-mini, Ministral, and Mistral-Small are instruction-tuned; Gemma-2 uses the -it variant. This heterogeneity is deliberate: we test whether results depend on the fine-tuning stage. Checkpoints up to 14 14 B run in bf16 on a single GPU. The 24 24 – 72 72 B models run in 4 4 - or 8 8 -bit, and a bf16-versus- 8 8 -bit control at 32 32 B confirms that quantization does not affect our conclusions (App. E ). All interventions use forward hooks on the residual stream and MLP layers.

sections.heading: 3.2 Recording and linear probes
sections.text: For population decoding we fit ridge probes with cross-validated regularization on the residual-stream activation at a token of interest, and predict a target variable (for the world map, the latitude and longitude of a city named in the prompt); probes are always scored on held-out items. For single-unit analyses we record MLP neuron activations (the input to down_proj ) and characterize each neuron’s tuning to a stimulus variable.

sections.heading: 3.3 Activation steering and residual-norm normalization
sections.text: To steer a concept (for example, Paris ) we build a direction d d as the mean residual of concept-bearing sentences minus a neutral baseline at a chosen layer, and inject α ​ d \alpha d into the residual stream. We read the effect on neutral prompts as the change in a target-versus-control log-probability contrast (for example, Paris-tokens versus Tokyo-tokens). Steering coefficients are conventionally reported in raw activation units and are not normalized across models ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ) . Because the residual-stream norm ‖ h ‖ ℓ \|h\|_{\ell} grows with model size, we express strength as a fraction of that norm, α = c ​ ‖ h ‖ ℓ \alpha=c\,\|h\|_{\ell} , which makes the intervention comparable across scales. Concept and control lists, stimuli, and probes are given in App. B .

sections.heading: 3.4 Specificity, directional, and null controls
sections.text: We standardize four choices that, left implicit, invalidate cross-model comparison. (R1) Held-out selection and evaluation : any neuron, direction, or hyperparameter is selected on one split and scored on a disjoint one. (R2) Comparable intervention units : steering directions are unit-normalized ( d ^ = d / ‖ d ‖ \hat{d}=d/\|d\| ) and their strength is the residual-norm fraction α = c ​ ‖ h ‖ ℓ \alpha=c\,\|h\|_{\ell} , so the actual injection is h ′ = h + c ​ ‖ h ‖ ℓ ​ d ^ h^{\prime}=h+c\,\|h\|_{\ell}\,\hat{d} and its norm is exactly c ​ ‖ h ‖ ℓ c\,\|h\|_{\ell} , a fixed fraction of the residual regardless of ‖ d ‖ \|d\| . The naive (uncorrected) pipeline omits both normalizations: it injects the raw mean-difference direction at a raw scalar coefficient, so the injection norm depends unpredictably on both ‖ d ‖ \|d\| and the model. (R3) Specificity and directional controls : a causal claim for a direction d d (target T T versus control C C ) must show that d d raises log ⁡ p ⁡ ( T ) − log ⁡ p ⁡ ( C ) \log p(T)-\log p(C) , that the control direction d C d_{C} reverses it, and that random directions do not. (R4) Nulls and confidence intervals : scores are compared against shuffled or pseudo-concept nulls and reported with bootstrap confidence intervals. A concept passes when all three R3 tests hold against the R4 null, and the pass-rate is the fraction of concepts that pass; alongside it we report the mean continuous specificity effect log ⁡ p ⁡ ( T ) − log ⁡ p ⁡ ( C ) \log p(T)-\log p(C) , which we treat as the primary metric (the pass-rate is grid-sensitive).

sections.heading: 3.5 Held-out operating-point selection
sections.text: The steering effect depends jointly on the intervention layer and the strength c c . Rather than fix these by hand, we select them the way the world-map probe selects its layer and regularizer: by held-out performance. We scan a (layer, strength) grid on part of the concepts and score the disjoint rest. For the main Qwen3 analysis we use 24 24 concepts across five categories (cities, persons, objects, animals, abstractions), a fine grid, and a four-fold split; the 24 24 – 72 72 B models use a coarser grid (App. C ).

sections.heading: 3.6 Lesioning and attribution
sections.text: To test language localization we locate language-selective neurons, ablate the top fraction, and measure the change in held-out next-token loss on each language. Neurons are ranked by gradient × \times activation attribution; as a robustness check we re-rank them by activation-magnitude difference between languages (App. C ). On models of 14 14 B and above the attribution backward pass exceeded memory because it allocated a full weight-gradient buffer; freezing all weights and marking only the recorded activations requires_grad removes that buffer while leaving the attribution numerically identical, so all 17 17 models are covered.

sections.heading: 3.7 Statistical procedures
sections.text: Effects carry bootstrap 95 % 95\% confidence intervals, resampled over concepts for steering and over sentences for lesioning. For the steering scaling question we regress the per-concept held-out effect on log 2 \log_{2} model size and report the slope with a bootstrap CI (a trend test). We restrict this regression to the Qwen3 ladder to hold family fixed; even so, its checkpoints are separate training runs rather than one model rescaled, so the slope estimates a trend across an empirical sequence of checkpoints, not a controlled effect of parameter count, and inherits whatever data- and recipe-differences distinguish those runs. For magnitude shape we correlate each neuron’s digit and spelled-out-word tuning curves (a cross-format test). Null distributions match the structure of each test (shuffled labels, pseudo-concepts).

sections.heading: An apparent scaling law.
sections.text: Steering coefficients are conventionally reported in raw, unnormalized units ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ) . Under this default pipeline, a raw mean-difference direction, a raw steering coefficient, and a first-token target probability, the effect grows monotonically across the Qwen3 ladder (Fig. 2 b): the gain rises from 0.6 0.6 B to 14 14 B, with exactly the shape one would report as an emergent capability.

sections.heading: Why it is an artifact.
sections.text: A raw steering coefficient is not a comparable unit of intervention. Across the Qwen3 ladder the residual-stream norm ‖ h ‖ ℓ \|h\|_{\ell} and the raw steering direction ‖ d ‖ \|d\| both vary substantially and non-monotonically with model size, and the fraction of the residual that a raw injection displaces, ‖ d ‖ / ‖ h ‖ \|d\|/\|h\| , swings between 0.12 0.12 and 0.27 0.27 with no clean dependence on scale (Fig. 2 a). A fixed raw coefficient therefore delivers a different, unpredictable intervention in each model, and any scaling law read from raw units reflects this incomparability rather than steerability. Normalizing the injection to the residual norm ( α = c ​ ‖ h ‖ \alpha=c\|h\| ) restores comparability. The argument is scale-independent: it shows the ruler is miscalibrated, not that larger models are less steerable, and the same confound distorts a 72 72 B comparison identically.

sections.heading: Dose-response and layer sensitivity.
sections.text: Under R2 the specificity-controlled effect is not monotone in strength but follows an inverted-U (Fig. 2 c): it rises, peaks at low-to-intermediate c c , then declines as stronger steering degrades the output distribution. The effect is also sharply layer-dependent (Fig. 8 ), rising with depth and peaking in late layers, so a single fixed layer, as used in most steering papers, can under- or over-state the effect. Any single-number “steering effect” is thus a point on two hidden axes.

sections.heading: A second confound: the operating point.
sections.text: With the specificity, directional, and null controls in place (R3–R4: the target direction must raise T T over control C C , the control direction must reverse it, random directions must not, all against a bootstrap null), a genuine direction-specific effect is present at every scale. Its apparent scaling , however, is set by where the intervention is applied. At a fixed, hand-picked operating point (layer 2 / 3 2/3 , strength 1 ⋅ ‖ h ‖ 1{\cdot}\|h\| ) the specificity pass-rate is erratic across the Qwen3 ladder ( 0.50 , 0.88 , 0.25 , 0.50 , 0.25 0.50,0.88,0.25,0.50,0.25 ; Fig. 2 d, grey), which naively reads as a collapse. Selecting the operating point on held-out concepts (Methods) and expanding to 24 24 concepts across five categories with bootstrap CIs gives a stable picture: the held-out pass-rate is 0.71 , 1.00 , 0.79 , 0.79 , 0.75 0.71,1.00,0.79,0.79,0.75 over 0.6 0.6 – 14 14 B, each 95 % 95\% CI above chance; the continuous specificity effect is significantly positive at every scale; and the slope of effect against log 2 \log_{2} size is + 0.31 +0.31 per doubling, 95 % 95\% CI [ − 0.11 , + 0.73 ] [-0.11,+0.73] —no significant scaling trend, though the CI does not exclude a moderate positive slope (Fig. 2 d, red). We read this as the absence of a detectable trend across this particular sequence of checkpoints, not as evidence that steerability is scale-invariant: the Qwen3 sizes are independently trained runs, so a homogeneous size axis is itself an assumption, and the test remains underpowered against the moderate slopes the interval still admits. Every model selects layer ≈ 0.8 \approx\!0.8 , never the hand-picked 2 / 3 2/3 , and concrete categories (objects, persons, cities) steer more strongly than abstract ones. No fixed operating point is comparable across models: both the apparent emergence and the apparent collapse are artifacts of that choice, removed only by selecting the operating point on held-out data.

sections.heading: Factor decomposition.
sections.text: To isolate which measurement choice drives the apparent scaling, we hold the metric (specificity contrast) and concept set ( 24 24 concepts) constant and vary two factors independently: unit normalization (raw vs. ‖ h ‖ \|h\| -normalized) and operating-point selection (fixed L ⋅ 2 / 3 L{\cdot}2/3 vs. held-out grid search). None of the four resulting cells shows a significant scaling trend (Fig. 6 ): raw+fixed slope + 0.22 +0.22 , 95 % 95\% CI [ − 0.02 , + 0.62 ] [-0.02,+0.62] ; normalized+held-out slope + 0.31 +0.31 , CI [ − 2.87 , + 4.05 ] [-2.87,+4.05] ; the other two are similarly flat. (The wider CIs in the decomposition relative to the main analysis reflect fewer probe prompts per concept—three vs. six—reducing per-concept precision; both use the same five models.) The apparent scaling in the naive pipeline (Fig. 2 b) therefore rests not on a single confound but on the compound of several uncalibrated choices—units, readout metric, and operating point—any one of which, when corrected, removes the trend.

sections.heading: The causal reading.
sections.text: Two observations sharpen it. First, the most concept-selective single MLP neurons are not sufficient levers: clamping one degrades output rather than inducing the concept, whereas a population direction does steer, an instance of the decodable ≠ \neq used gap ( Elhage et al., 2022 ) ; Fig. 10 (App. D ) shows real steered generations, in which a Paris direction bends a neutral story toward the Eiffel Tower while staying fluent. Second, held-out evaluation matters: in-sample single-neuron concept selectivity ( d ′ ≈ 6 d^{\prime}\!\approx\!6 on a representative model) roughly halves out of sample ( d ′ ≈ 2 d^{\prime}\!\approx\!2 ), with several concepts falling below the pseudo-concept null. sections.heading: 4.3 Magnitude coding and number neurons
sections.text: Every model contains strong magnitude tuning: the best number-tuned neuron reaches held-out r = 0.68 r=0.68 – 0.98 0.98 , far above null, in all 17 17 models up to 72 72 B (Fig. 3 a; the 32 32 B bf16-versus- 8 8 -bit control is identical). Whether these neurons look bell-shaped or monotonic, however, is entirely a matter of selection. Ranking neurons by linear correlation with number—the natural first choice, and the one that recovers biological number-neuron studies— returns only monotonic units, because a linear criterion cannot rank an interior-peaked tuning curve highly. A shape-agnostic criterion (a held-out quadratic fit; App. C ) tells a different story: bell-shaped (interior-peak, negative quadratic coefficient) number neurons are present in every model (hundreds to thousands among all well-tuned units), and are common among the top 30 30 in Llama, Phi, and Mistral, mixed in Gemma, and rare-to-absent in the top 30 30 for Qwen (Fig. 3 b; fractions are threshold-sensitive, App. C ). Are these genuine numerosity units or digit-token detectors? A cross-format test asks whether a neuron keeps its tuning curve when the number is a digit (“ 17 17 ”) or a spelled-out word (“seventeen”). The bell units are partly format-invariant in Llama, Phi, and Mistral (cross-format tuning correlation 0.59 0.59 – 0.70 0.70 , above each model’s random-neuron baseline of 0.30 0.30 – 0.51 0.51 , with 73 73 – 83 % 83\% of bell units keeping r > 0.5 r>0.5 ; the margin over random is large in Phi but modest in Ministral; App. C ), a split that holds to 72 72 B (Llama-70B and Mistral-24B r ≈ 0.7 r\approx 0.7 , Qwen monotonic-dominant), which indicates numerical-magnitude tuning beyond pure token identity, though not fully invariant and weaker in Qwen. Fig. 11 (App. D ) shows a real bell-shaped neuron whose digit and word curves nearly coincide. Magnitude is therefore strongly encoded, but the code is mixed : monotonic units alongside partly format-invariant bell units, in a family-dependent mix rather than a clean monotonic-only line. An efficient-coding argument (App. A ) shows why a monotonic code would be optimal for frequency-weighted discrimination ( Laughlin and others, 1981 ; Dehaene, 2003 ; AlquBoj et al., 2025 ) , but that is a normative prediction the models only partly follow, not a description of what they do. (b) Under shape-agnostic neuron selection, bell-shaped number neurons appear, common in Llama/Phi/Mistral and rare in Qwen; the linear-correlation selection that returned “ 0 % 0\% bell” was biased.

sections.heading: 4.4 Language localization
sections.text: Locating language-selective neurons by gradient × \times activation attribution, ablating the top fraction, and bootstrapping the held-out loss over 44 44 sentences per language (App. C ), the Chinese half is robust: Chinese-selective ablation hurts Chinese significantly more than English in all 17 17 tested models ( 95 % 95\% CI > 0 >0 everywhere). The English half is not. English selectivity is statistically indistinguishable from zero in 12 12 of 17 17 models (CI straddles 0 0 ; Fig. 4 a) and significantly positive in only five (Qwen3-0.6B, Ministral-8B, Qwen3-32B, Qwen2.5-72B, Gemma-2-27B). A full double dissociation, with both halves significant and positive, therefore holds in only 5 5 of 17 17 models. However, the formal ablated-language × \times test-language interaction (zh_sel + + en_sel, with CIs combined in quadrature) is significantly positive in all 17 17 models: language-selective ablation hurts the targeted language more than the non-targeted one everywhere, even when the per-language selectivities individually fail to reach significance. Even this asymmetry is attribution-dependent , and this is our cleanest single instance of measurement-dependence. Gradient × \times activation ranks a neuron by its causal importance (how much perturbing it changes the loss), whereas activation magnitude ranks it by how strongly it fires for a language; the two diverge because a unit can be highly active for a language without being causally load-bearing, the same decodable ≠ \neq used gap that undercuts single directions (§ 4.1 ). Under the activation-magnitude ranking the asymmetry flips: Chinese is significant in only 7 / 9 7/9 models (two Qwen fail) while English becomes significant in 7 / 9 7/9 (App. C ). The only claim robust to both the bootstrap and a change of attribution is the weakest one: some language-specific structure is localizable in most models, but which language, how cleanly, and in which direction depend on which notion of “importance” the analyst picks. At scale, gradient × \times activation keeps Chinese significant to 72 72 B. English selectivity is significant in both large Qwen models but in neither Mistral-24B nor Llama-70B, and its magnitude is erratic (Qwen3-32B + 3.7 +3.7 vs. Qwen2.5-72B + 0.5 +0.5 ); we read this as further model-dependence, not a scale effect. This is the one parallel consistent across all tested checkpoints (Table 2 ); Fig. 13 (App. D ) plots the recovered coordinates, which reproduce global geography. Its robustness is not a counterexample to our thesis but a confirmation of it: the world map is the only one of the four tasks that is pure decoding , with no intervention, no single-neuron selection, and no operating-point choice, so none of the three artifact classes (unit incomparability, operating-point drift, selection bias) can reach it. sections.heading: 5 Discussion
sections.text: Across four experiments (Table 2 ) a single pattern holds: rigor is decisive exactly where selection and intervention enter (concept steering, lesions) and inert for purely correlational decoding (the world map), which is consistent to 72 72 B. Each headline parallel weakens under its matching control. The steering “emergence” rests on two confounds, raw units and an arbitrary operating point; choosing that point on held-out data leaves steerability significant at every scale with no detectable trend. The magnitude “monotonic code” is a selection effect: shape-agnostic selection finds bell-shaped neurons in every model. The lesion “double dissociation” survives neither a bootstrap nor a change of attribution method; the formal interaction is significant everywhere, but whether the per-language halves individually hold depends on method and model. This is not an argument that parallels between LLMs and brains are false: geography is robustly mapped, magnitude robustly encoded, concepts genuinely steerable, and Chinese reliably localizable. It is an argument that the field’s binding constraint is comparability and controls : an unaudited probe or intervention tends to over-claim, and a single arbitrary knob—a layer, a selection rule, a sample size—can fabricate a scaling law, a coding shape, or a functional map.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: Although all experiments extend to 72 72 B, the densest scale analysis is limited to the Qwen lineage up to 14 14 B; larger models use coarser grids and quantized inference, though a 32 32 B bf16-versus- 8 8 -bit control shows closely matched results. The 24 24 -concept steering set limits precision, and broader coverage would better constrain scaling trends. Number-neuron results remain partly format-dependent, and non-symbolic stimuli would better separate magnitude from symbol identity. Family and scale effects are also not fully separable, since model families do not share a common size grid. Accordingly, the absence of a significant steering trend should be interpreted as no detectable trend rather than evidence of no trend. Construct validity could be strengthened through leave-name-out steering and non-lexical evaluation, while mean ablation and larger language test sets would further validate the lesion results. Finally, residual-norm normalization improves comparability but does not guarantee equal functional dose across models, and our analysis is limited to representational rather than dynamical phenomena.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: Treating LLMs as objects of neuroscience is productive only with neuroscience-grade controls. A deep case study shows an apparent causal scaling law to be an artifact of intervention units and an arbitrary operating point. A cross-generation audit to 72 72 B then finds that, of three further parallels, only the linear world map is consistent across all tested checkpoints: the magnitude “monotonic code” was a selection bias, and the language “double dissociation” does not survive bootstrap and attribution-method controls. We release the protocol, grid, stimuli, and code so that future “LLMs also show X X ” claims can be scored, not merely asserted.

sections.heading: Appendix A Derivation: the magnitude code is the CDF of number frequency
sections.text: Let a model represent number n n by a scalar coordinate ϕ ⁡ ( n ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \phi(n)\in[0,1] read out with fixed resolution (additive noise σ \sigma in ϕ \phi -space); numbers occur with frequency p ⁡ ( n ) p(n) and training rewards discriminating them in proportion to p p . The number of distinguishable levels near n n is ∝ ϕ ′ ​ ( n ) / σ \propto\phi^{\prime}(n)/\sigma , so expected discriminability ∫ p ⁡ ( n ) ​ log ⁡ ( ϕ ′ ​ ( n ) / σ ) ​ 𝑑 n \int p(n)\,\log\!\big(\phi^{\prime}(n)/\sigma\big)\,dn is maximized subject to ∫ ϕ ′ ​ ( n ) ​ 𝑑 n = 1 \int\phi^{\prime}(n)\,dn=1 by the Lagrange condition p ⁡ ( n ) / ϕ ′ ​ ( n ) = const p(n)/\phi^{\prime}(n)=\text{const} : ϕ ′ ​ ( n ) ∝ p ⁡ ( n ) ⟹ ϕ ⁡ ( n ) = ∑ m ≤ n p ⁡ ( m ) = F ⁡ ( n ) , \phi^{\prime}(n)\propto p(n)\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad\phi(n)=\!\!\sum_{m\leq n}\!p(m)=F(n), the CDF of p p (histogram equalization / optimal companding; Laughlin and others, 1981 ). For heavy-tailed text statistics p ⁡ ( n ) ∝ 1 / n p(n)\!\propto\!1/n , ϕ ⁡ ( n ) ∝ log ⁡ n \phi(n)\!\propto\!\log n : a monotone log-compressed line with constant Weber fraction Δ ​ n / n \Delta n/n . Within this idealized model (scalar code, additive read-out noise, reward ∝ \propto frequency) the optimum is monotone for any p > 0 p>0 , so a bell-shaped (non-monotone) code is sub-optimal. This is a statement about the idealized population coordinate , not about single-neuron tuning: our shape-agnostic analysis (§ 4.3 ) shows individual neurons can be bell-shaped, so the derivation is a normative prediction of the optimal code, not a description of the LLM’s units.

sections.heading: Appendix D Qualitative examples
sections.text: This appendix gives one concrete, real example per experiment, so the aggregate statistics have a face. Fig. 10 shows what a steering intervention actually does to the text. Every row is a real, greedy-decoded output of Llama-3.1-8B for the same prompt, with a concept direction added to the residual stream at layer ≈ 0.8 \approx\!0.8 depth (Methods); the injected concept vocabulary is highlighted. Unsteered, the model writes a neutral vignette. Adding the Paris direction at a moderate strength ( c = 0.2 c\!=\!0.2 ) bends the same story toward Paris (“Parisian street,” the “Eiffel Tower”) while staying fluent, and the Dolphin direction pulls the same opening to the sea (“waves of the ocean,” “salty air”). Figure 10: What steering does, in words (real Llama-3.1-8B generations, one fixed prompt). A concept direction added to the residual stream injects that concept’s vocabulary (highlighted) while the sentence stays coherent at a moderate coefficient. The last row shows over-steering ( c = 0.35 c\!=\!0.35 ): the same direction now dominates and the text collapses into repetition, the free-generation face of the inverted-U dose-response in Fig. 2 c. The fluent band is concept-dependent, so a single fixed coefficient is not comparable across concepts.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2608.08159v1 [cs.AI] 08 Aug 2026 When Is a Steerable Concept Representation Real? Measurement Confounds in a Cross-Family Audit of Neuroscience Parallels in LLMs Yuqi Wu Affiliation: College of Biomedical Engineering, Fudan University Shengming Zhao Affiliation: College of Biomedical Engineering, Fudan University Jie Chen † † thanks: Correspondence, jc65ualberta.ca Affiliation: College of Biomedical Engineering, Fudan University Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly reported to exhibit human-like neural and cognitive signatures, including concept cells, mental number lines, and cognitive maps. These claims often rely on linear probing and activation steering applied to a single model, yet both methods are highly sensitive to measurement choices. A reported parallel may therefore reflect the model, the measurement procedure, or both. We audit four representative neuroscience-inspired paradigms across 17 models from five families, spanning 0.6 0.6 B to 72 72 B parameters. Our main experiment examines the causal steerability of concept directions. With raw activation units and a fixed layer and coefficient, steerability appears to increase with model scale, resembling an emergent capability. However, this pattern is produced by an uncalibrated pipeline rather than by a claim established in the steering literature. The trend depends jointly on raw units, the readout metric, and the operating point; correcting any one of these removes it. With residual-norm-comparable interventions and held-out operating-point selection, concept steering remains significant at every scale, but shows no significant trend across the Qwen3 series, although the confidence interval does not rule out a moderate positive slope. The remaining results are mixed. A linear geographic world map is consistently decodable in every tested checkpoint up to 72 72 B. Number magnitude is strongly encoded, but whether individual neurons appear bell-shaped or monotonic depends on the selection criterion. Language-specific structure is localizable, but the direction of the cross-lingual asymmetry reverses under a different attribution method. These results suggest that the main constraint on AI neuroscience is not a lack of phenomena, but a lack of comparable measurements and adequate controls. We release the protocol, stimuli, and code. 1 Introduction Figure 1: Same data, different ruler, different conclusion. Left: a standard pipeline makes concept steerability appear to increase with model size in raw activation units. Once the intervention is normalized across models and the operating point is selected on held-out concepts, no significant scaling trend remains. Right: the four neuroscience-inspired phenomena examined in this study and the conclusions supported after control analyses. A growing body of “AI neuroscience” treats large language models (LLMs) as systems whose internal representations can be recorded and perturbed. This literature has reported several parallels with biological cognition, including neurons selective for individual concepts ( Quiroga et al., 2005 ; Templeton et al., 2024 ) , linear representations of space and time ( Gurnee and Tegmark, 2024 ) , log-compressed number representations with Weber–Fechner behaviour ( AlquBoj et al., 2025 ; Nieder, 2016 ) , and emotion or concept directions that causally influence model outputs ( Sofroniew et al., 2026 ; Rimsky et al., 2024 ) . Together, these findings suggest that LLMs may exhibit representational structures resembling those observed in biological systems. Many such results rely on two methods: linear probing , which tests whether a variable can be decoded from activations, and activation steering , which tests whether adding a direction changes model behaviour. Both are sensitive to analytical choices, including how units are selected, how intervention strength is defined, which layer is used, and whether specificity and null controls are included. Moreover, most studies examine a single model or a narrow range of model sizes. This makes it difficult to distinguish model-specific findings from broader regularities, or genuine effects from measurement artifacts. Similar concerns have already been raised for emergent capabilities, some of which disappear under alternative metrics ( Schaeffer et al., 2023 ) . Here, we examine the same problem in a causal representational setting. We examine concept steering in depth and audit three additional neuroscience-inspired phenomena across 17 models from five families, spanning 0.6 0.6 B to 72 72 B parameters. Rather than asking whether these phenomena are “real” in an absolute sense, we test whether the associated claims remain stable under stronger controls and alternative measurement choices. For concept steering (§ 4.1 ), the apparent increase with model scale is not measurement-invariant: it depends jointly on raw intervention units, the readout metric, and a fixed operating point, and disappears when any one of these is corrected. With residual-norm-comparable interventions and held-out operating-point selection, steering remains significant at every tested scale, but shows no significant trend across the Qwen3 series. We formalize these controls in an audit protocol (§ 3 ) combining held-out selection, residual-norm normalization, specificity and null controls, and cross-family replication. Applied across all four analyses, the protocol yields a cross-model taxonomy (§ 4 ): linear geographic structure is consistently decodable up to 72 72 B; number magnitude is robustly encoded, but bell-shaped versus monotonic tuning depends on neuron selection; and language-specific structure is localizable, although the direction of the cross-lingual asymmetry changes with the attribution method. We further derive an efficient-coding account of monotonic magnitude representations under an idealized scalar model (App. A ) and release the protocol, stimuli, and code. 1 1 1 Anonymized: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ai-neurosci-audition-45CF (de-anonymized upon acceptance). 2 Related Work Cognitive parallels in LLMs. LLMs linearly encode space and time ( Gurnee and Tegmark, 2024 ) , task-specific world models ( Li et al., 2023a ) , truth ( Marks and Tegmark, 2023 ) , and number magnitude, reproducing distance/size/ratio effects and a log-compressed number line ( AlquBoj et al., 2025 ; Dehaene, 2003 ; Nieder, 2016 ) ; emotion, concept, and persona directions have been characterized and steered ( Sofroniew et al., 2026 ; Templeton et al., 2024 ) . These works establish that the relevant geometry exists. We ask which causal claims survive controls across families and scales. Probing and steering. Linear probes read variables off activations ( Alain and Bengio, 2017 ) , but a decodable variable need not be one the model uses, which is why control-task baselines are needed ( Hewitt and Liang, 2019 ) . Steering methods add a direction to change behaviour: difference-in-means and contrastive activation addition ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ) , activation addition ( turner2023activation ) , inference-time intervention ( Li et al., 2023b ) , and representation engineering ( Zou et al., 2023 ) ; the linear representation hypothesis ( Park et al., 2024 ) underpins most causal claims, and factual edits localize to MLP weights ( Meng et al., 2022 ) . Crucially, the steering literature does not claim that steerability emerges with scale: Rimsky et al. (2024) report mixed effects at 13 13 B, and the one systematic cross-scale study ( Ali et al., 2025 ) finds that CAA effectiveness diminishes with model size. The apparent emergence our case study examines is therefore a natural default, not an established claim; because an unnormalized recipe can manufacture either an apparent rise or an apparent decline, raw units are not a comparable measure of steerability across scale. Superposition ( Elhage et al., 2022 ) , dictionary learning ( Bricken et al., 2023 ) , and cross-model convergence ( Huh et al., 2024 ) warn that decodable directions need not be the units of computation, a warning we operationalize. The reliability of steering vectors is itself an active concern, and our units argument gives one concrete failure mode. Neuroscience anchors. Concept cells ( Quiroga et al., 2005 ) ; place and grid cells ( O’Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971 ; Hafting et al., 2005 ; Constantinescu et al., 2016 ) ; the geometry of abstraction ( Bernardi et al., 2020 ) ; efficient coding ( Laughlin and others, 1981 ) ; and bell-shaped number neurons provide the biological referents against which we score the models. 3 Methods 3.1 Models and grid We evaluate 17 17 open-weight checkpoints spanning five developers, from 0.6 0.6 to 72 72 B parameters: Qwen3 at { 0.6 , 1.7 , 4 , 8 , 14 , 32 } \{0.6,1.7,4,8,14,32\} B and Qwen2.5- 72 72 B; Llama-3.2 at { 1 , 3 } \{1,3\} B, Llama-3.1- 8 8 B, and Llama-3.1- 70 70 B; Phi-3.5-mini ( 3.8 3.8 B) and Phi-4 ( 14 14 B); Ministral- 8 8 B and Mistral-Small- 24 24 B; and Gemma-2 at { 9 , 27 } \{9,27\} B. Qwen3/Qwen2.5 and Phi-4 are base (pre-trained) checkpoints; Llama, Phi-3.5-mini, Ministral, and Mistral-Small are instruction-tuned; Gemma-2 uses the -it variant. This heterogeneity is deliberate: we test whether results depend on the fine-tuning stage. Checkpoints up to 14 14 B run in bf16 on a single GPU. The 24 24 – 72 72 B models run in 4 4 - or 8 8 -bit, and a bf16-versus- 8 8 -bit control at 32 32 B confirms that quantization does not affect our conclusions (App. E ). All interventions use forward hooks on the residual stream and MLP layers. 3.2 Recording and linear probes For population decoding we fit ridge probes with cross-validated regularization on the residual-stream activation at a token of interest, and predict a target variable (for the world map, the latitude and longitude of a city named in the prompt); probes are always scored on held-out items. For single-unit analyses we record MLP neuron activations (the input to down_proj ) and characterize each neuron’s tuning to a stimulus variable. 3.3 Activation steering and residual-norm normalization To steer a concept (for example, Paris ) we build a direction d d as the mean residual of concept-bearing sentences minus a neutral baseline at a chosen layer, and inject α ​ d \alpha d into the residual stream. We read the effect on neutral prompts as the change in a target-versus-control log-probability contrast (for example, Paris-tokens versus Tokyo-tokens). Steering coefficients are conventionally reported in raw activation units and are not normalized across models ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ) . Because the residual-stream norm ‖ h ‖ ℓ \|h\|_{\ell} grows with model size, we express strength as a fraction of that norm, α = c ​ ‖ h ‖ ℓ \alpha=c\,\|h\|_{\ell} , which makes the intervention comparable across scales. Concept and control lists, stimuli, and probes are given in App. B . 3.4 Specificity, directional, and null controls We standardize four choices that, left implicit, invalidate cross-model comparison. (R1) Held-out selection and evaluation : any neuron, direction, or hyperparameter is selected on one split and scored on a disjoint one. (R2) Comparable intervention units : steering directions are unit-normalized ( d ^ = d / ‖ d ‖ \hat{d}=d/\|d\| ) and their strength is the residual-norm fraction α = c ​ ‖ h ‖ ℓ \alpha=c\,\|h\|_{\ell} , so the actual injection is h ′ = h + c ​ ‖ h ‖ ℓ ​ d ^ h^{\prime}=h+c\,\|h\|_{\ell}\,\hat{d} and its norm is exactly c ​ ‖ h ‖ ℓ c\,\|h\|_{\ell} , a fixed fraction of the residual regardless of ‖ d ‖ \|d\| . The naive (uncorrected) pipeline omits both normalizations: it injects the raw mean-difference direction at a raw scalar coefficient, so the injection norm depends unpredictably on both ‖ d ‖ \|d\| and the model. (R3) Specificity and directional controls : a causal claim for a direction d d (target T T versus control C C ) must show that d d raises log ⁡ p ⁡ ( T ) − log ⁡ p ⁡ ( C ) \log p(T)-\log p(C) , that the control direction d C d_{C} reverses it, and that random directions do not. (R4) Nulls and confidence intervals : scores are compared against shuffled or pseudo-concept nulls and reported with bootstrap confidence intervals. A concept passes when all three R3 tests hold against the R4 null, and the pass-rate is the fraction of concepts that pass; alongside it we report the mean continuous specificity effect log ⁡ p ⁡ ( T ) − log ⁡ p ⁡ ( C ) \log p(T)-\log p(C) , which we treat as the primary metric (the pass-rate is grid-sensitive). 3.5 Held-out operating-point selection The steering effect depends jointly on the intervention layer and the strength c c . Rather than fix these by hand, we select them the way the world-map probe selects its layer and regularizer: by held-out performance. We scan a (layer, strength) grid on part of the concepts and score the disjoint rest. For the main Qwen3 analysis we use 24 24 concepts across five categories (cities, persons, objects, animals, abstractions), a fine grid, and a four-fold split; the 24 24 – 72 72 B models use a coarser grid (App. C ). 3.6 Lesioning and attribution To test language localization we locate language-selective neurons, ablate the top fraction, and measure the change in held-out next-token loss on each language. Neurons are ranked by gradient × \times activation attribution; as a robustness check we re-rank them by activation-magnitude difference between languages (App. C ). On models of 14 14 B and above the attribution backward pass exceeded memory because it allocated a full weight-gradient buffer; freezing all weights and marking only the recorded activations requires_grad removes that buffer while leaving the attribution numerically identical, so all 17 17 models are covered. 3.7 Statistical procedures Effects carry bootstrap 95 % 95\% confidence intervals, resampled over concepts for steering and over sentences for lesioning. For the steering scaling question we regress the per-concept held-out effect on log 2 \log_{2} model size and report the slope with a bootstrap CI (a trend test). We restrict this regression to the Qwen3 ladder to hold family fixed; even so, its checkpoints are separate training runs rather than one model rescaled, so the slope estimates a trend across an empirical sequence of checkpoints, not a controlled effect of parameter count, and inherits whatever data- and recipe-differences distinguish those runs. For magnitude shape we correlate each neuron’s digit and spelled-out-word tuning curves (a cross-format test). Null distributions match the structure of each test (shuffled labels, pseudo-concepts). 4 Experiments and Results 4.1 The “concept steerability emerges with scale” finding is a measurement artifact An apparent scaling law. Steering coefficients are conventionally reported in raw, unnormalized units ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ) . Under this default pipeline, a raw mean-difference direction, a raw steering coefficient, and a first-token target probability, the effect grows monotonically across the Qwen3 ladder (Fig. 2 b): the gain rises from 0.6 0.6 B to 14 14 B, with exactly the shape one would report as an emergent capability. Why it is an artifact. A raw steering coefficient is not a comparable unit of intervention. Across the Qwen3 ladder the residual-stream norm ‖ h ‖ ℓ \|h\|_{\ell} and the raw steering direction ‖ d ‖ \|d\| both vary substantially and non-monotonically with model size, and the fraction of the residual that a raw injection displaces, ‖ d ‖ / ‖ h ‖ \|d\|/\|h\| , swings between 0.12 0.12 and 0.27 0.27 with no clean dependence on scale (Fig. 2 a). A fixed raw coefficient therefore delivers a different, unpredictable intervention in each model, and any scaling law read from raw units reflects this incomparability rather than steerability. Normalizing the injection to the residual norm ( α = c ​ ‖ h ‖ \alpha=c\|h\| ) restores comparability. The argument is scale-independent: it shows the ruler is miscalibrated, not that larger models are less steerable, and the same confound distorts a 72 72 B comparison identically. Dose-response and layer sensitivity. Under R2 the specificity-controlled effect is not monotone in strength but follows an inverted-U (Fig. 2 c): it rises, peaks at low-to-intermediate c c , then declines as stronger steering degrades the output distribution. The effect is also sharply layer-dependent (Fig. 8 ), rising with depth and peaking in late layers, so a single fixed layer, as used in most steering papers, can under- or over-state the effect. Any single-number “steering effect” is thus a point on two hidden axes. A second confound: the operating point. With the specificity, directional, and null controls in place (R3–R4: the target direction must raise T T over control C C , the control direction must reverse it, random directions must not, all against a bootstrap null), a genuine direction-specific effect is present at every scale. Its apparent scaling , however, is set by where the intervention is applied. At a fixed, hand-picked operating point (layer 2 / 3 2/3 , strength 1 ⋅ ‖ h ‖ 1{\cdot}\|h\| ) the specificity pass-rate is erratic across the Qwen3 ladder ( 0.50 , 0.88 , 0.25 , 0.50 , 0.25 0.50,0.88,0.25,0.50,0.25 ; Fig. 2 d, grey), which naively reads as a collapse. Selecting the operating point on held-out concepts (Methods) and expanding to 24 24 concepts across five categories with bootstrap CIs gives a stable picture: the held-out pass-rate is 0.71 , 1.00 , 0.79 , 0.79 , 0.75 0.71,1.00,0.79,0.79,0.75 over 0.6 0.6 – 14 14 B, each 95 % 95\% CI above chance; the continuous specificity effect is significantly positive at every scale; and the slope of effect against log 2 \log_{2} size is + 0.31 +0.31 per doubling, 95 % 95\% CI [ − 0.11 , + 0.73 ] [-0.11,+0.73] —no significant scaling trend, though the CI does not exclude a moderate positive slope (Fig. 2 d, red). We read this as the absence of a detectable trend across this particular sequence of checkpoints, not as evidence that steerability is scale-invariant: the Qwen3 sizes are independently trained runs, so a homogeneous size axis is itself an assumption, and the test remains underpowered against the moderate slopes the interval still admits. Every model selects layer ≈ 0.8 \approx\!0.8 , never the hand-picked 2 / 3 2/3 , and concrete categories (objects, persons, cities) steer more strongly than abstract ones. No fixed operating point is comparable across models: both the apparent emergence and the apparent collapse are artifacts of that choice, removed only by selecting the operating point on held-out data. Factor decomposition. To isolate which measurement choice drives the apparent scaling, we hold the metric (specificity contrast) and concept set ( 24 24 concepts) constant and vary two factors independently: unit normalization (raw vs. ‖ h ‖ \|h\| -normalized) and operating-point selection (fixed L ⋅ 2 / 3 L{\cdot}2/3 vs. held-out grid search). None of the four resulting cells shows a significant scaling trend (Fig. 6 ): raw+fixed slope + 0.22 +0.22 , 95 % 95\% CI [ − 0.02 , + 0.62 ] [-0.02,+0.62] ; normalized+held-out slope + 0.31 +0.31 , CI [ − 2.87 , + 4.05 ] [-2.87,+4.05] ; the other two are similarly flat. (The wider CIs in the decomposition relative to the main analysis reflect fewer probe prompts per concept—three vs. six—reducing per-concept precision; both use the same five models.) The apparent scaling in the naive pipeline (Fig. 2 b) therefore rests not on a single confound but on the compound of several uncalibrated choices—units, readout metric, and operating point—any one of which, when corrected, removes the trend. The causal reading. Two observations sharpen it. First, the most concept-selective single MLP neurons are not sufficient levers: clamping one degrades output rather than inducing the concept, whereas a population direction does steer, an instance of the decodable ≠ \neq used gap ( Elhage et al., 2022 ) ; Fig. 10 (App. D ) shows real steered generations, in which a Paris direction bends a neutral story toward the Eiffel Tower while staying fluent. Second, held-out evaluation matters: in-sample single-neuron concept selectivity ( d ′ ≈ 6 d^{\prime}\!\approx\!6 on a representative model) roughly halves out of sample ( d ′ ≈ 2 d^{\prime}\!\approx\!2 ), with several concepts falling below the pseudo-concept null. (a) The units confound: the raw injection fraction ‖ d ‖ / ‖ h ‖ \|d\|/\|h\| varies non-monotonically across the Qwen3 ladder, so a fixed raw coefficient is an uncontrolled intervention. (b) In raw units the effect nonetheless appears to grow monotonically with scale, an apparent emergent capability. (c) Under residual-norm normalization with specificity control, the strength dose-response is an inverted-U, not monotone growth (colour = = size). Red and grey come from different selection pipelines and are not point-for-point comparable. 4.2 Steerability across scale and a quantization control Extending the held-out analysis to the large models (Table 1 ), the held-out effect is significantly positive at every large scale, with a bootstrap 95 % 95\% CI above 0 0 for all five (Gemma-2-27B + 22.9 ​ [ + 18.5 , + 27.1 ] +22.9\,[+18.5,+27.1] , Qwen2.5-72B + 7.1 ​ [ + 6.0 , + 8.3 ] +7.1\,[+6.0,+8.3] , Qwen3-32B + 4.9 ​ [ + 2.7 , + 7.2 ] +4.9\,[+2.7,+7.2] , Mistral-24B + 5.5 ​ [ + 4.5 , + 6.4 ] +5.5\,[+4.5,+6.4] , Llama-70B + 4.5 ​ [ + 3.0 , + 6.1 ] +4.5\,[+3.0,+6.1] ), so steering does not vanish at scale. Whether these neurons look bell-shaped or monotonic, however, is entirely a matter of selection. Ranking neurons by linear correlation with number—the natural first choice, and the one that recovers biological number-neuron studies— returns only monotonic units, because a linear criterion cannot rank an interior-peaked tuning curve highly. A shape-agnostic criterion (a held-out quadratic fit; App. C ) tells a different story: bell-shaped (interior-peak, negative quadratic coefficient) number neurons are present in every model (hundreds to thousands among all well-tuned units), and are common among the top 30 30 in Llama, Phi, and Mistral, mixed in Gemma, and rare-to-absent in the top 30 30 for Qwen (Fig. 3 b; fractions are threshold-sensitive, App. C ). Are these genuine numerosity units or digit-token detectors? A cross-format test asks whether a neuron keeps its tuning curve when the number is a digit (“ 17 17 ”) or a spelled-out word (“seventeen”). The bell units are partly format-invariant in Llama, Phi, and Mistral (cross-format tuning correlation 0.59 0.59 – 0.70 0.70 , above each model’s random-neuron baseline of 0.30 0.30 – 0.51 0.51 , with 73 73 – 83 % 83\% of bell units keeping r > 0.5 r>0.5 ; the margin over random is large in Phi but modest in Ministral; App. C ), a split that holds to 72 72 B (Llama-70B and Mistral-24B r ≈ 0.7 r\approx 0.7 , Qwen monotonic-dominant), which indicates numerical-magnitude tuning beyond pure token identity, though not fully invariant and weaker in Qwen. Fig. 11 (App. D ) shows a real bell-shaped neuron whose digit and word curves nearly coincide. Magnitude is therefore strongly encoded, but the code is mixed : monotonic units alongside partly format-invariant bell units, in a family-dependent mix rather than a clean monotonic-only line. An efficient-coding argument (App. A ) shows why a monotonic code would be optimal for frequency-weighted discrimination ( Laughlin and others, 1981 ; Dehaene, 2003 ; AlquBoj et al., 2025 ) , but that is a normative prediction the models only partly follow, not a description of what they do. Figure 3: Magnitude: strong tuning, mixed shape. (a) Held-out magnitude tuning is strong in every model, to 72 72 B. (b) Under shape-agnostic neuron selection, bell-shaped number neurons appear, common in Llama/Phi/Mistral and rare in Qwen; the linear-correlation selection that returned “ 0 % 0\% bell” was biased. 4.4 Language localization Locating language-selective neurons by gradient × \times activation attribution, ablating the top fraction, and bootstrapping the held-out loss over 44 44 sentences per language (App. C ), the Chinese half is robust: Chinese-selective ablation hurts Chinese significantly more than English in all 17 17 tested models ( 95 % 95\% CI > 0 >0 everywhere). The English half is not. English selectivity is statistically indistinguishable from zero in 12 12 of 17 17 models (CI straddles 0 0 ; Fig. 4 a) and significantly positive in only five (Qwen3-0.6B, Ministral-8B, Qwen3-32B, Qwen2.5-72B, Gemma-2-27B). A full double dissociation, with both halves significant and positive, therefore holds in only 5 5 of 17 17 models. However, the formal ablated-language × \times test-language interaction (zh_sel + + en_sel, with CIs combined in quadrature) is significantly positive in all 17 17 models: language-selective ablation hurts the targeted language more than the non-targeted one everywhere, even when the per-language selectivities individually fail to reach significance. Even this asymmetry is attribution-dependent , and this is our cleanest single instance of measurement-dependence. Gradient × \times activation ranks a neuron by its causal importance (how much perturbing it changes the loss), whereas activation magnitude ranks it by how strongly it fires for a language; the two diverge because a unit can be highly active for a language without being causally load-bearing, the same decodable ≠ \neq used gap that undercuts single directions (§ 4.1 ). Each headline parallel weakens under its matching control. The steering “emergence” rests on two confounds, raw units and an arbitrary operating point; choosing that point on held-out data leaves steerability significant at every scale with no detectable trend. The magnitude “monotonic code” is a selection effect: shape-agnostic selection finds bell-shaped neurons in every model. This is not an argument that parallels between LLMs and brains are false: geography is robustly mapped, magnitude robustly encoded, concepts genuinely steerable, and Chinese reliably localizable. It is an argument that the field’s binding constraint is comparability and controls : an unaudited probe or intervention tends to over-claim, and a single arbitrary knob—a layer, a selection rule, a sample size—can fabricate a scaling law, a coding shape, or a functional map. Limitations. Although all experiments extend to 72 72 B, the densest scale analysis is limited to the Qwen lineage up to 14 14 B; larger models use coarser grids and quantized inference, though a 32 32 B bf16-versus- 8 8 -bit control shows closely matched results. The 24 24 -concept steering set limits precision, and broader coverage would better constrain scaling trends. Number-neuron results remain partly format-dependent, and non-symbolic stimuli would better separate magnitude from symbol identity. Family and scale effects are also not fully separable, since model families do not share a common size grid. Accordingly, the absence of a significant steering trend should be interpreted as no detectable trend rather than evidence of no trend. Construct validity could be strengthened through leave-name-out steering and non-lexical evaluation, while mean ablation and larger language test sets would further validate the lesion results. Finally, residual-norm normalization improves comparability but does not guarantee equal functional dose across models, and our analysis is limited to representational rather than dynamical phenomena. 6 Conclusion Treating LLMs as objects of neuroscience is productive only with neuroscience-grade controls. A deep case study shows an apparent causal scaling law to be an artifact of intervention units and an arbitrary operating point. A cross-generation audit to 72 72 B then finds that, of three further parallels, only the linear world map is consistent across all tested checkpoints: the magnitude “monotonic code” was a selection bias, and the language “double dissociation” does not survive bootstrap and attribution-method controls.
